why.support: Online, people can't see your face. Words can land hard. Learn to disagree with **reasons, not insults**. Learn to stand up for people, and when to report.
why.core: Online, there's no face and no tone of voice, so messages land harder than we mean them to. The words you choose can turn a disagreement into a fight, or calm it down. Learning to disagree with **reasons, not insults**, to stand up for someone, and to know when to report or walk away keeps you, and the people around you, safer.
why.extend: Online interaction strips away the cues (voice, face, timing) that soften disagreement, so language carries all the weight. Choosing how forceful to be, supporting claims with reasons, recognising implied meanings and knowing the reporting pathways let you take part in online spaces without escalating harm.

articles.title: Disagree without losing it

body.support:
Group chats, game chats, comments: arguments happen online.

**Why they blow up.** Online, people can't see your face or hear your **tone**. Words land harder.

**1. Pause.** Read it again.

**2. Turn it down.** *That's so dumb* starts a fight. *I see it differently* doesn't.

**3. Reasons, not insults.** Say what you think, and **why**. Ask a question.

**4. Walk away from trolls.** **Trolls** post to make people angry. Block them.

**5. Be an upstander.** Message the person privately. Don't share the mean post. **Report** it.

**6. Report serious stuff.** Screenshot it. Report it to the app. Tell an adult. If it's not removed in **48 hours**, tell **eSafety**.

In danger? Call **000**. Kids Helpline: 1800 55 1800.
body.core:
Group chats, game chats, comment sections: online is where a lot of arguments happen. Even if you're under 16 and off apps like TikTok and Instagram, you're probably still in group chats, on Discord or playing games with chat.

**Why online arguments blow up.** Online, there's no face, no **tone** of voice, and no chance to say *I'm joking*. So messages often land harder than people mean. And once it's posted, other people can join in, and a small disagreement can turn into a **pile-on**.

**1. Pause.** Read the message again. Could it mean something else? Are you about to send something you wouldn't say to their face?

**2. Turn it down.** Words can be more or less forceful. *This is the dumbest take I've ever seen* and *I see it differently* make the same point, but one starts a fight.

**3. Reasons, not insults.** Disagree with the **idea**, not the person. Say what you think and **why**. *I like that game because the updates keep it fresh.* Ask a question: *What do you like playing instead?*

**4. Know when to walk away.** Some people post just to make others angry. They're called **trolls**. Replying gives them what they want. Block, mute or leave the chat.

**5. Be an upstander.** If someone's being targeted, you can help. Send them a private message. Post something kind. Don't like or share the hurtful post. And **report** it.

**6. Report what's serious.** If it's bullying, threats or someone's private photos:

- Take a **screenshot**.
- Report it to the app or platform.
- Tell an adult you trust.
- If you're under 18 and it's serious cyberbullying, and the platform doesn't remove it within **48 hours**, you can report it to **eSafety**.

If anyone is in danger, call **000**. For someone to talk to, Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800) is free, any time.
body.extend:
Much conflict now happens in text-based spaces: group chats, gaming platforms and comment sections. Under-16s, now restricted from holding accounts on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, still use messaging and gaming services with chat.

**Why online disagreement escalates.** Text removes the cues that soften face-to-face talk: facial expression, **tone** of voice, timing. Readers fill the gaps, often assuming hostility. Public replies invite others in, and disagreement can become a **pile-on**.

**1. Pause and re-read.** Consider other possible meanings, and what's **implied** as well as stated.

**2. Adjust force.** Evaluative language can be graded: *This is the dumbest take I've ever seen* versus *I see it differently*. Lower-force language keeps the point but invites a reply rather than a fight.

**3. Substantiate.** Target the idea, not the person, and give **reasons** or evidence. Questions keep a discussion open.

**4. Disengage from trolling.** Content designed to provoke rewards replies. Block, mute or leave.

**5. Act as an upstander.** Support the person privately or publicly, don't amplify the harmful content, and **report** it.

**6. Use reporting pathways.** For serious harm: screenshot, report to the platform, and tell a trusted adult. Under eSafety's cyberbullying scheme, people under 18 can complain to **eSafety** if serious cyberbullying isn't removed by the platform within **48 hours**.

If anyone is in danger, call **000**. Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800) is free and available any time.

caseStudies.title: What teens face online

body.support:
**eSafety** is a government group that helps keep people safe online. It asked **627 teens** about being online. That was in **2020**.

What it found:

- **44%** had something bad happen online in six months.
- For teens aged **14 to 17**, it was **more than half**.
- Common problems: messages from **strangers**, seeing upsetting stuff, and being **left out**.

So if it's happened to you, you're not alone.

If someone bullies you online, report it to the app. If it's not removed in **48 hours**, tell **eSafety**.
body.core:
**eSafety** is the government agency that helps keep Australians safe online. It asked **627 Australian teens** aged 12 to 17 about their online lives. It shared what it found in **2021**.

Here's what it found:

- **44%** of teens had a **negative** experience online in the six months before the survey (to September 2020).
- For teens aged **14 to 17**, it was **more than half**.
- The most common problems were:
  - being contacted by a **stranger** (30%)
  - seeing **upsetting or unwanted content** (20%)
  - being **left out** by others (16%).

So if something bad has happened to you online, you're not alone. And being **left out** counts too: it hurts, even when no one says anything mean.

eSafety also runs a **cyberbullying scheme** for under-18s. First, report the post to the platform. If serious cyberbullying isn't taken down within **48 hours**, you can make a complaint to eSafety, and it can step in.
body.extend:
**eSafety**, Australia's online safety regulator, surveyed **627 Australian teenagers** aged 12 to 17 about their digital lives. It published the results in **2021**.

- **44%** had a **negative** online experience in the six months to September 2020.
- Among **14 to 17 year olds**, it was **over 50%**.
- The most common experiences were contact from a **stranger** (30%), **unwanted content** (20%) and being **excluded** (16%).

The data show negative experiences are common, not rare. They also show that harm isn't only abuse. Being **left out** is one of the most common experiences, and it can happen without a single mean word.

eSafety's **cyberbullying scheme** helps under-18s when platforms don't act. First, report the content to the platform. If serious cyberbullying isn't removed within **48 hours**, you can complain to eSafety.

**The comment:** “Anyone who likes this team is an idiot.”

**My reply:** I see it differently. They lost on Saturday, but they have won six of their last eight games. I think the new coach is doing a good job. What makes you say that?

**Standing up for someone:** Hey, that comment about Ava's photo was not OK. Ava, I think it is a great shot.

**When I would report instead:** If the comments turned into threats, or went on for days, I would not reply. I would screenshot, report and block.

teacher.overview: Students learn why online disagreement escalates (no face, tone or timing; public audiences; pile-ons) and how to respond: pausing, grading the force of evaluative language, disagreeing with the idea rather than the person, substantiating claims with reasons, disengaging from trolls, acting as upstanders and using reporting pathways (screenshot, report to the platform, tell a trusted adult, and eSafety's cyberbullying scheme for under-18s after 48 hours). The case study is eSafety's research on Aussie teens' negative online experiences. Under-16s are now restricted from major social media platforms, so the course uses group chats and game chats as its main settings.
prep: Know your school's procedures for online bullying and disclosures before you start.
Have support details visible: Kids Helpline (1800 55 1800), your wellbeing team, eSafety.
Choose low-stakes example topics (games, sport, music) for practice. Avoid making students argue about their identities.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** no face or tone, readers assume the worst, others can join in. Upstander: message privately, post something kind, don't share, report. Reporting: screenshot, report to the platform, tell a trusted adult, then eSafety after 48 hours for under-18s.

**Reply:** 1 acknowledge; 2 I-statement; 3 reason; 4 question; 5 restraint (no insults, no screenshots); 6 result (it calmed down).

**Turn it down (samples):** *I think you might be missing how the new rules work*; *I actually like it, but I know it's not for everyone*; *I don't agree. Can I explain why?*; *That feels like a generalisation. Not everyone thinks that way.*

**Sort:** strategy feedback — reply; rumour — report (and support); troll — walk away; threat — report (adult, 000 if danger); racist joke — reply (call it out calmly) and report if it continues; ignoring stop — report (block, tell an adult).

**Case study:** contact from a stranger (30%), unwanted content (20%), exclusion (16%); exclusion signals you don't belong, even silently; report to the platform first; if serious cyberbullying isn't removed within 48 hours, under-18s can complain to eSafety.

realityCheck: **This can bring up real experiences.** Some students are being bullied right now, or are doing the bullying. Keep examples general, and follow up privately.
**Don't force public disagreement about identity.** Use low-stakes topics for practice.
**Racism and hate.** Calling it out is good, but safety comes first. Make reporting and telling an adult equally valid choices.
**The research is from 2020.** It was collected before the social media age restrictions. Mention that online life has changed since, but the patterns still apply in group chats and games.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's directly useful, and the rewriting work is a strong language lesson.
